topics.title: Colonial arrival chronology
topics.summary: The surviving evidence for when John Gurney reached New England: at Weymouth by 30 May / 2 June 1641, arrived 1638–early 1641, bounded below by his original Weymouth land grants and above by the post-1640 falloff of the Great Migration.

topics.title: Colonial Weymouth community
topics.summary: John's first New England years, roughly 1638/9–1642/4, as an admitted inhabitant of Weymouth: town-granted land in the East and Mill Fields, a credit tie to the town's minister, documented associates among the founding settlers, and the thin limit of his militia footprint.

topics.title: Colonial Braintree community
topics.summary: John's settled colonial home from about 1645 to his death in 1662/3: the 1645 plantation petition, the fifteen-year tenancy of William Tyng's farm (the future Adams family seat), his own Monatiquot River freehold, his tailor's trade, and his standing among Braintree neighbours.

topics.title: Colonial frontier rights
topics.summary: The proprietary rights John took up in newly-forming inland plantations in his last years, 1659–1663 — a Billerica house-lot and proprietor's share, a Mendon allotment, and the unlocated Quinapaug interest carried into his estate — none of which became his residence.

topics.title: Colonial material life
topics.summary: The material texture of John's life read from his 1663 estate inventory: an all-movable estate of £55 14s 6d held mostly in livestock and the gear of a working farm, a sparse but sufficient household, and not one tool of the tailoring trade his deeds name him by.

topics.title: Colonial record coverage
topics.summary: The shape of John's surviving documentary footprint: a dense 1641–1663 civic, land, court, and probate trail across four towns, with no vital or church record fixing his own person and no surviving record stating his English origin, parentage, or prior residence.

topics.title: Family — wives and marriages
topics.summary: John's two marriages: Mary, married in England by the mid-1620s, mother of all his children, died at Braintree 20 September 1661; and the much-married widow Grizzell three weeks later — with the misread "John Cheny" Braintree town record resolved as John Gurney.

topics.title: Family — the children as a family group
topics.summary: John Gurney's children reconstructed as a family group: a five-child roster — Sarah, Mary, Richard (the direct-line G12), John Jr., and Peter — with Isaac a probable but unproven sixth, all born to his first wife Mary, assembled from the compiled Braintree and Gurney genealogies, cross-checked against Torrey's marriage compendium, and anchored child by child in scattered land, court, and probate records.

topics.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy
topics.summary: John Gurney Jr.'s Mendon household with his wife Ruth and their children John, Samuel, and Mary: his death in the 1675 Mendon massacre, Ruth's swift remarriage to John Bundy of Taunton, the resolution of which same-named John cousin actually died there, the separate post-1667 Mendon proprietary lots of John Jr. and his father's widow Grisel, Peter's King Philip's War service and 1676 death, and two open leads on a further Taunton-area descendant trail.

topics.title: Family — colonial collaterals
topics.summary: Colonial-era same-surname Gurneys outside John's documented family: the Providence, Rhode Island John and Sarah Gurney (1695-1714), real but unconnected by any surviving record, with Torrey's compendium offering a plausible but unconfirmed grandson reading; an unresolved Suffolk Deeds index entry for a James Gurner; and a third apparent thread at colonial Dorchester resolved as the unrelated Gurnell family, not a Gurney.

topics.title: Origin — age and baptism
topics.summary: The chronology of John's own age and birth, triangulated from four handles of unequal strength: his 1652/3 deposition 'aged 50 or thereabouts' (a decade-rounded self-report), the identity work's probable East Dereham baptism (c.1609/10), the bound set by his daughter Mary's 1647 marriage, and the September 1611 marriage of his likely parents — which sit in friction rather than agreement. The three birth-year estimators overlap around a probable window of 1604–1608 inside a possible 1602–1610, and his own baptism stays unproven on independent evidence.

topics.title: Origin — trade and training
topics.summary: The origin bearing of John's tailoring trade. A tailor's craft usually passed father to son, and his likely father Francis Gurney was a Merchant Taylor from a Norfolk textile family — so his training should be traceable, yet both formal pathways (the Merchant Taylors' Company of London and the Norwich freemen and apprentice registers) carry no John Gurney in the emigrant window. His craft was learned off the enrolled books; the trade points back toward a Norfolk textile family, strengthening without proving the Norfolk and Francis association.

topics.title: Origin — migration and reception network
topics.summary: How John Gurney reached and joined the New England community, read from the colonial record: reception into an already-settled Weymouth land-and-neighbour network rather than a documented shared voyage; an unrecorded crossing whose passenger-list silence is what Great-Migration timing (the thin 1639–41 tail) predicts; and the reception network as a weak lever for English origin — except for the geographic affinity that makes adjacent Hingham, settled from the Gurneys' own Norfolk parishes, the one reception corridor fitting the favoured origin, an argument held to the identity work.

topics.title: Origin — wardship and patronage network
topics.summary: The English wardship-and-patronage network around the senior West Barsham branch in John's emigration decade: the branch as a Court of Wards minor-heir household under the widowed Martha Lewkenor, and the 1627 Gurdon–Winthrop letter placing 'Mrs. Gurney' inside the Court of Wards circle of Winthrop and Downing. Read as origin-bearing context about the senior branch that neither connects John to it nor traces his crossing, with the identity question held to the case file.

topics.title: Origin — Bury connections
topics.summary: Charles Banks's 'Bury St Edmunds' attribution — the one specific English parish any published authority ever named for John — resolved: an unproven 'Banks Mss.' lead with no Bury natal record behind it, most plausibly tracking the feltmaker John Newgate's 1636 runaway apprentice rather than the emigrant, and consistent with the favoured Norfolk origin. The Bury registers hold no Gurney household that could have fathered him, and Anderson independently records the origin as 'Unknown'.

topics.title: Origin — traditions
topics.summary: Two family traditions weighed for what they are worth: the American 1615-birth and Southwark-origin tradition, retold across three compilations a century apart, explained as the true biography of the 1636 Newgate apprentice misattached to the older Braintree emigrant, alongside a separate, uncorroborated Elm Street Cemetery burial-place lead; and the Gurney colonial-arms tradition, resting on a blazon genuinely attested in Norfolk itself but with no early American physical witness yet found.

topics.title: Identity — candidate overview
topics.summary: The shared matching-criteria profile and elimination scaffold the case file applies across every alternative English John Gurney candidate: of 51 same-name households surveyed, three principal alternatives and 45 further households are eliminated on structural grounds and five are held to a low residual, leaving Candidate B the sole survivor. The case file's own probability model for Candidate B stays external-canonical there, cross-referenced rather than restated; what the elimination amounts to is the assessment unit.

topics.title: Identity — Candidate A: Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire
topics.summary: Candidate A's continuous Buckinghamshire/Northamptonshire chain — the 1603 Stewkley baptism, the 1628 Bierton marriage to Alice Oliffe, the 1638-1653 Aylesbury family group, and a 1641 move into Northamptonshire — places one Englishman in England across exactly the years the Massachusetts John Gurney was at Weymouth and Braintree. A wider Bucks Gurney household map and a 1661 Edlesborough marriage independently reinforce the elimination.

topics.title: Identity — Candidate B: Norfolk parentage
topics.summary: The surviving candidate's own case: John Gurney of Braintree as the son of Francis Gurney, Merchant Taylor, by Margaret Rybett of Norfolk. Two primary records carry it — the 1611 Norwich marriage no earlier genealogist found, and the East Dereham baptism re-read from "Nicholas Gorne" to "John the sonne of ffrancis Gurnie" — supported by a father-to-son trade, the East Anglia-to-London corridor, and Rivett and West Barsham kin close by. Against them: the 1633 Visitation's "eldest sonne," no English marriage record, and a deposition age too old. Probable, not proven.

topics.title: Identity — Candidate D: London Draper, Old Change
topics.summary: Candidate D — John Gurney, son and executor of Robert Gurney, citizen and draper of Old Change — is eliminated: the same John Gurney is documented continuously in the same St Augustine Watling Street parish from a 1638 rents return through a 1662 hearth-tax entry, the same year the colonial John of Braintree was dying at Boston; the missing wife Mary and matching children give the elimination a second, independent ground.

topics.title: Identity — Ackworth, Yorkshire
topics.summary: The 1636 Ackworth marriage of John Gurnoe to Mary Burton is the only same-name comparator anywhere in the record sweeps whose wife is genuinely named Mary in roughly the right window — held at a residual ~3% rather than eliminated outright, capped by a naming/birth-order mismatch and the colonial John's own pre-1628 marriage bound.

topics.title: Identity — Other Eliminations and Earsham
topics.summary: A 1638 Earsham, Norfolk Gurney yeoman family (wife Mary, son John too young to be the emigrant); the distinct Gurnell surname; a six-parish Norfolk household-density survey; a targeted Richard/Isaac negative search; and the wider English probate, parish, and muster comparators that clear the remaining same-name field, leaving Candidate B the sole surviving identity.

topics.title: Identity — assessment
topics.summary: What the identity work adds up to: an identification reached by elimination and circumstantial fit rather than by any document naming John's father. Eliminates the last principal alternative (Candidate C, Berkhamsted); states the unknown-corridor residual the eliminations do not clear; leaves open whether John emigrated through the Gurdon–Winthrop patronage network; reads Anderson's "Boston" settlement as a conflation with the 1636 Newgate apprentice; and names the two end-states for the estimate and the three levers that would move it.

topics.title: Research-state source coverage
topics.summary: The state of the online search beyond the FamilySearch, Internet Archive, and Google corpus: the specialist emigrant compilations, digitized colonial-church indexes, and Massachusetts aggregators searched for John Gurney, and what each returned.

topics.title: Research-state open questions
topics.summary: The standing unresolved questions of the John Gurney research program: his English origin and parentage, the identity and English marriage of his first wife Mary, and the untested Y-DNA discriminator — reconciled against the canonical research-leads catalogue.
